triplets.head: Ophthalmotilapia ventralis "Longola"
triplets.tail: Maternal mouthbrooder that must be kept in a harem structure — one male with several females. Males are highly aggressive toward other males. Harem dissipates male courtship aggression. Different color morphs must not be mixed as they hybridize freely.

triplets.head: Neolamprologus pulcher
triplets.tail: Suitable for group breeding (cooperative breeder, group structure essential)

triplets.head: Neolamprologus pulcher
triplets.tail: One of the best-known cooperative breeders among cichlids. Lives in permanent social groups of one breeding pair plus 1–14 helpers of both sexes. Group breeding is biologically essential as helpers assist with brood care, territory defense, and predator vigilance. Highly territorial toward unfamiliar conspecifics (dear enemy effect).

triplets.head: Neolamprologus helianthus
triplets.tail: Needs careful mixed farming (pair-forming, aggressive to conspecifics)

triplets.head: Neolamprologus helianthus
triplets.tail: Territorial cave spawner very aggressive toward conspecifics. Start with group of ≥6 juveniles for natural pair formation but subdominants are not tolerated and must be removed. Once a dominant pair forms they bond for life. Multiple generations of fry can coexist with parents. Multiple adult pairs require very large tank with separated territories.

triplets.head: Tropheus Moorii "Golden firefox"
triplets.tail: Suitable for group breeding (large colony mandatory)

triplets.head: Tropheus Moorii "Golden firefox"
triplets.tail: Maternal mouthbrooder with extreme conspecific aggression that can only be managed through large group size of 15–20+ individuals. In smaller groups (5–6) fish fight to the death. Each male needs ~60 cm territory with rock pile and 6–10 females per male. New individuals must never be added to established colony.

triplets.head: Cyphotilapia frontosa
triplets.tail: Suitable for group breeding (gregarious colony/harem structure)

triplets.head: Cyphotilapia frontosa
triplets.tail: Gregarious maternal mouthbrooder that should be kept in groups of at least 5, ideally 10+. Males are polygynous (each needs 3–4 females). Unlike most cichlids, males do not hold distinct territories but form a dominance hierarchy within the group. Non-territorial social structure makes them well-suited for group keeping. Females brood for 35–50+ days with unique buccal feeding behavior.
